text.p: Following are highlights of the main stories in Croatian newspapers on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified them and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- What will be on the agenda at the meeting of president Franjo Tudjman and chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency Alija Izetbegovic? Diplomatic sources say: municipalities inside the Croat-Moslem federation, work of Bosnian state television, law on citizenship and use of the (Croatian) port of Ploce.

- Political parties debate what to do about the International War Crimes Tribunal's subpoena to Croatia to hand over some documents. Social Democrats ask for urgent session of parliament, while Istrian Democratic Union suggests handing over part of the requested documentation.

- Ater a series of mafia-style street killings in Zagreb, Interior Minister Ivan Penic says Croatia is still one of the safest countries in transition and has more policemen than is standard in Europe.

- Croatia prepares to reform its pension system, which will tend to replace a state-guaranteed pension with individual arrangements, including premium life insurance that beneficiaries can start paying when they are thirty.
- The first transit centre offering temporary accommodation for expatriate Croats coming back to Croatia after living abroad, will soon be opened on the outskirts of Zagreb.

- No cheap beds in Zagreb. The capital has five high-class hotels, several middle class and only one in the cheapest category. But apart from the luxury hotels, others have similar prices, regardless of the quality they offer.

- Under new regulations banks that go bankrupt must pay back to savers their deposits of up to 30,000 kuna in full, or 75 percent of amounts from 30,000-50,000 kuna. As sums larger than 50,000 kuna cannot be insured, analysts believe savers will seek to divide their money and deposit several smaller sums with different banks.

- Of some 350,000 potential beneficiaries of voucher privatisation, 95,000 have registered so far. Registration, which ends on October 2, is expected to pick up pace now that refugees have received the necessary certificates.

- A lot of companies undergoing privatisation, whose value was overestimated by the Privatisation Fund, are asking the Fund to decrease their capital. Many hoteliers are devaluing shares while other companies are withdrawing treasury shares.

- Industrial output and employment are on a constant decrease in Zagreb and have reached the level of thirty years ago. However, Zagreb dominates Croatia's foreign trade, participating in 38 percent of the country's overall exports and 58 percent of imports.

- Croatia's Economy Minister Nenad Porges says foreign investors have not been put off by the IMF/World Bank's postponement of loans. "Serious investment groups and corporations have sufficient information about Croatia and are not at all impressed by these political pressures".
- Talks between Zagreb and the American company Bechtel, contracted to build a Zagreb-Split motorway, had not broken down but are stalled over the issue of financing the project.

- Croatian companies trade freely inside Bosnia. But problems arise when they want to invest in Bosnian Moslem territory. Many firms which had assets inside Bosnia before the war, now find those assets have been confiscated.

- Ericsson Tesla signed a 56 million kuna contract with state telecom HPT, to deliver state of the art telephone switchboards and other telecommunication equipments to the Serb-populated Eastern Slavonia enclave, which returns to Croatian rule after six years of separatism. -- Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
